A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Graph Alignment via Birkhoff Relaxation. Their main texts, equations, figures, references, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching proofs moved into v2's appendices.

before.justification: V1 Section 5 and Figure 1 report original Gaussian Wigner simulations comparing Birkhoff, Simplex, and GRAMPA, including matching accuracy and distance from the true permutation.

after.justification: V2 retains the original simulation comparisons and adds empirical phase-transition thresholds and a fitted scaling exponent in Section 5 and Figure 2.

M1.justification: The Birkhoff objective, doubly stochastic constraints, Gaussian input model, and rounding procedures remain unchanged. Hungarian projection was already used in v1's simulations. V2's regularized eigenvalue-gap construction changes the proof, not the algorithm.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate synthetic Gaussian Wigner graph alignment over the same graph-size and noise ranges. V2's finer noise sampling examines retained coverage; discussions of other applications and non-GOE matrices do not introduce evaluations on those domains.

E2.justification: Figure 1 compares Birkhoff with the same Simplex and GRAMPA methods in both versions. EIG1 appears in v2's new theoretical comparison table, but is not added to the empirical comparison.

E3.justification: V2 adds a phase-transition experiment using a 0.01 noise increment, locating where normalized Frobenius distance reaches 0.5 across graph sizes. V1 reports the coarser 0.1 sweep. The existing comparison's solver, GRAMPA regularization, rounding, and principal settings are retained.

E4.justification: V2 adds a focused finite-size scaling analysis asking whether the distance transition follows an inverse-square-root noise threshold. Figure 2 estimates transition locations across graph sizes, extending v1's accuracy and distance-versus-noise analyses.

E5.justification: V2 introduces linear regression of log noise thresholds against log graph size to estimate the scaling exponent in Figure 2. Ten-run averaging for Figure 1 remains unchanged, and neither version provides confidence intervals, significance tests, or seed identifiers.

E6.justification: V2 adds low-noise samples in Figure 1's center panel and reports a fitted transition exponent of -0.450 in Figure 2. The retained comparisons preserve the reported ranking of Birkhoff above Simplex and GRAMPA; the added results concern transition scaling rather than a same-setting performance improvement.

T1.justification: Theorem 1 changes the sufficient condition from sigma <= n^(-1.25-epsilon), with squared-distance bound 8n^(1-epsilon/8), to sigma <= n^(-1-epsilon), with bound 10n^(1-epsilon/32). Section 4 and Appendix C.3 supply a substantially revised regularized eigenvalue-gap argument. New Corollary 3 and Appendix A also establish near-complete recovery through Hungarian projection.

C1.justification: The abstract, main contributions, and conclusion strengthen the claimed near-complete recovery regime from sigma = o(n^-1.25) to sigma = o(n^-1). This materially enlarges the central theoretical guarantee. The well-separation claim around n^-0.5 and the claim of state-of-the-art guarantees for Birkhoff relaxation remain.

C2.justification: V2 newly discusses generalization beyond GOE: Section 3.1 identifies concentration conditions sufficient for well-separation, while Remark 8 identifies eigenvector concentration as the recovery-proof bottleneck. It also interprets the new fitted exponent as support for inverse-square-root transition scaling. Existing qualifications about rounding and the unresolved sharp recovery threshold remain.

D1.justification: V2 Section 5 supplies a code-repository address and newly reports CPU execution, 50 GB of memory, and a three-hour limit per instance. These are additional disclosures; the PDFs do not establish a change to the earlier experiments' computing budget. CVXPY, SCS, use_indirect, and GRAMPA's 0.2 regularization were already documented.

R1.justification: V2 expands practical motivation with references including Aflalo, Birdal and Simsekli, Fogel, and Lyzinski, and adds Gaudio for broader graph-isomorphism context. Feng's Small gaps of GOE reference disappears with the revised proof. Explicit comparator formulations and Table 1 clarify positioning, while the central relationship to GRAMPA and Simplex remains.

P1.justification: V2 substantially reorganizes the proof exposition: rounding proofs, well-separation estimates, the commutator bound, and eigenvector-concentration details are grouped into Appendices A-C, while Section 4 focuses on the central lemma. The introduction and related-work explanations expand, and author information and citation style change.

P2.justification: The document adopts a different conference-style layout with a redesigned title and author block, changed typography and spacing, and removal of running headers. V2 adds Table 1 and Figure 2, relocates Figure 1 into the simulation discussion, and updates its center-panel title and sampling display.

improvement.justification: V2 resolves the improvement toward an n^-1 noise regime explicitly left prospective in v1 Section 4 through a worked revision of the eigenvalue-gap proof. It also establishes a guarantee for the Hungarian rounding used experimentally and adds direct scaling evidence and reproducibility disclosures. These substantially strengthen the theoretical contribution and its support, although the conjectured n^-0.5 recovery threshold remains open.
